claims.text: Pulumi's component state migrations let component authors ship an upgrade path with the component itself; a migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change.
The Pulumi component state migrations API is experimental and may change.
A GitHub discussion for feedback on component state migrations exists at github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ covering component state migrations and the callback contract.
The pulumi/examples repository contains the directory aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration with v1, v2, and v3 programs and migration code, with a README for v1.
The pulumi/examples repo contains migration files at aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts and v3/migration.ts.
A link to Pulumi docs page /docs/iac/concepts/components/ describes components.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/aliases/ describing aliases.
The legacy AWSX VPC component is `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc`, and it manages the VPC, subnets, route tables, and gateways.

In the example's v1, the `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component creates a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway; a security group sits outside the component and refers to the VPC.
Per the AWS CloudFormation EC2 SecurityGroup documentation for VpcId, changing a security group's VPC requires replacing the security group.

Without a migration connecting old state to new code, upgrading from legacy to modern AWSX could replace the VPC instead of keeping it, and a new VPC would mean replacing the security group too because the security group refers to the VPC's ID.
If a database is recreated, its replacement does not automatically contain the old data; without a backup or data migration deleting the old database could mean losing the data.
The modern AWSX component is `awsx.ec2.Vpc`; the example's v3 removes AWSX and declares the resources directly with `@pulumi/aws`.
Across all three versions of the example, the AWS resource IDs stay the same and the security group continues to use the same VPC.

In the example's resource trees, v1 uses component types awsx:x:ec2:Vpc, awsx:x:ec2:Subnet and awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway; v2 uses awsx:ec2:Vpc with managed aws resources as children (subnet named vpc-isolated-1); v3 uses plain aws resources only.
Pulumi's state records both physical resources and components; each record has a Pulumi name called a URN, and managed resources also have a provider ID such as an AWS VPC ID.

Legacy AWSX wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components, while modern AWSX removes those wrappers and puts managed resources under different parents; the subnet's Pulumi name changes from `vpc-isolated-0` to `vpc-isolated-1`.

Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible, but cannot by themselves remove component wrappers and transfer references to replacement resources; a state migration handles that whole change together.
A component registers a state migration by passing an alias for the legacy component type and a migration callback through the `stateMigrations` resource option.

A state migration callback receives the saved state of the aliased old component followed by the state of its children, and returns `newState` (the complete set of records replacing the old component and its children) and `successors` (a map from each old URN that disappears to the URN that takes its place).
The example's migration callback is idempotent: if the state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources it does nothing, and an unexpected component type raises an error.
The example's `rename` helper copies the saved record and changes its URN, type, and parent while preserving the AWS resource ID and other saved fields.

The `successors` entries let the Pulumi engine update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack, so the security group's reference to the VPC remains valid after migration and retains the same AWS VPC ID.

The example's v3 migration removes the AWSX VPC component record and moves the managed VPC into its place; both the old component and its VPC child map to the new VPC record, and the VPC keeps its AWS ID.

Pulumi runs multiple state migration callbacks in order, passing each result to the next callback; a stack on legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to plain AWS, a stack on modern AWSX skips the first migration, and after both have run both callbacks return no result on later updates.
Keeping earlier migrations with the component lets users skip versions without editing stack state by hand.

After a state migration, Pulumi compares the new program with the migrated state and calls the provider for remaining changes; the example can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags.

Running `pulumi preview` before each upgrade should show no creates, deletes, or replacements for the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group; preview evaluates the migration without saving it, and the update saves the migrated state.

When a component registers its own state migration, users do not need to write the migration, attach the callback, or edit stack state; Pulumi runs the migration as part of the normal preview and update when they upgrade the component.
For an internal component change that keeps the same inputs and outputs, users can keep their existing component calls without knowing which resources moved.
Pulumi's component state migrations are new, and shipping the migration with the component makes the upgrade path part of the reusable building block, written and tested once for all teams.
Pulumi state migration callbacks (the state migrations resource option) run during previews and updates when prior state exists.
Pulumi state migration callbacks must be idempotent and must return no result when the state no longer needs migration.
Pulumi state migration callbacks rewrite resource state without performing provider operations.
A Pulumi component state migration is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A Pulumi component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings.
In a Pulumi component state migration result, each successor mapping connects an old URN that is omitted from the result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, a Pulumi component state migration callback returns no result.
The Pulumi component state migration callback state entries use the checkpoint resource format, including fields such as `urn`, `type`, `id`, `parent`, `provider`, `inputs`, and `outputs`.
The Pulumi option reference page at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/statemigrations/ has a callback API section that explains the callback API.
A component state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using Pulumi update plans or targeted updates.
The restrictions on state-changing migration results during Pulumi update plans or targeted updates do not require removing an already-applied component state migration.
